About

Todd leads Zonda's Building Products Advisory and research practice, where our team aims to publish the most thoughtful and diligent research on the industry.

Todd is the architect behind a number of publicly cited industry measures and analysis, and has a reputation as one of the most careful researchers in the housing/building products industry.

Before joining Zonda, Todd led JBREC Building Products Repair/Remodel forecasts, and economic/industry forecasting for North America at Kohler Co. Todd is an 11-time winner of the most accurate category forecaster from the Chicago Federal Reserve. Todd's analysis is regularly cited by various media, including the Wall Street Journal, CNBC, New York Times, and others.

Distribution will increasingly skew to companies exposed to 'existing housing stock', rather than new homes. Why this matters:

1) Macro drivers that drive building products revenue skew differently as industry revenue tilts to existing homes vs new. 

Change in mortgage rates or income growth? Different impact to overall distribution revenue vs earlier cycles. Consider: most executives in these companies have a good sense of what housing starts their revenue projection is based on, but have less clear idea of what real income growth or HELOC assumptions are built in (if at all). That needs to flip.

2) Its not so easy to do 'both' halfhearted. Physical footprint of products used on existing homes is often different than new homes. Labor plays a different role too. Different SKUs, different contractors, usually different margins. 

The bottom line: Underlying distribution of building products will likely be quite different 2030-40 as the market adjusts.

PS: An academic paper a few years ago from Fed researchers compared 'superstar markets' (like San Fran - hard to build, but high home price appreciation) with 'easier to build' markets like Atlanta. 
The finding was that delays, higher marginal costs, uncertainty, reduce supply elasticity. Which means home price volatility is amplified, and so is mix of supply from existing vs new. More 'new' housing units comes from retrofit of older housing stock (or conversion) rather than taking all that land risk.

The distribution of who wins in that environment looks quite different too. Thats the point.

I’m increasingly skeptical when building products companies tell me they are ‘taking luxury market share’. Here is why:
Last weekend I had dinner with arguably the best cabinet maker in Nantucket. The type that was born into the work, and locals would recognize immediately. I was struck by the conversation

His instinct for lumber pricing was remarkable. Unlike framing materials, hardwood pricing is a low-information market (i.e. illiquid market, poor pricing data, little/no exchange traded contracts on future prices for species). Yet he had worked out complex pricing problems. Do you have a good sense of how tariff changes will impact European Oak, including who bears the risk and when? He did. Quite impressive.

He was remarkably adept at switching suppliers and materials. He seemed to have an instinct (including entirety of NYC area) of which suppliers had inefficiencies in inventory/procurement, and was quite clever in how to navigate.

Was totally open to shopping new suppliers, including the large names with historically poor service. Because of perceptions of mispricing. That’s interesting.

Now imagine you are a supplier trying to capture market share of this pro. Who in your organization is actually making decisions?
- A generalist product or channel manager with several years experience in the category? 
- Working with limited data/perception of differences in regional pricing 
- Poor real time data on end-market ‘lux’ customers (i.e. generic segmentations rather than live job data)
-  Shifting distribution, but without clear understanding of counterparties involved
-  Very imperfect pricing model

Here is the point: in luxury markets, there is what economists call ‘information asymmetry’. Local markets are dominated by a few highly informed professionals who are very close to a small geography. 

As a result, luxury growth plays out very unevenly, and is extremely susceptible to ‘pro-veto’ by the parties closest to the project. Most manufacturers who think they are capturing ‘luxury market share’ overestimate their ability to win. 

That’s the theme playing out in Q3, as companies point to luxury growth. Leadership should looking for evidence of durable gains, which are harder won. 

PS – what was also clear is the Lux market is shifting (yet again). His company was getting calls suppliers who would call him ahead of price increases. Some pull forward in Lux materials ahead of price increase.

PPS - its plausible that AI could drive some future efficiency gains in Lux distribution, precisely because AI can measure some of these hard to capture datapoints at scale (with cost involved). Down the road.

To watch: Spend on household durables just gained ground vs recreation services for two quarters in a row. Intriguing because:

1) Its a shift against long-term trend of growing HH spend growth on recreation services vs 'things' in the home.

2) Its unusual (less than 15% odds of this happening sequentially), and historically occurred near periods of POSITIVE turning points in residential construction. 

3) The 'Vibe Shift' towards housing was historically unusual in these periods. For example, in 1972/73 there was a perception that future demand would be 'endless' due to wave of boomers forming households (prior to stagflation). Similar with 1998-2006 perception of tech boom / housing opulence. Very different than how things have felt the past few years.

If we hadn't seen the data, would you have guessed this shift was occurring? I would not. 

But this is plausibly one check-mark in the 'turning point near' argument for increased spend on housing durables / home improvement, etc. 

Worth noting: odds of this 'randomly' stretching into 3 quarters trend is very low (20:1 against). If spend on durables grows vs recreation services sequentially next quarter too, it would seem to be evidence that home improvement rebound amid all that deferral is turning.

Are you seeing this 'in the wild' at all? People you know spending on things in their homes while cutting back on recreation spend? Examples welcome.

Cross your fingers. Watching closely.

"These Aren't the Contractors You're Used To" 
Construction startups just jumped +22% per dollar of addressable spending. Why you should care:

For the past ~25 years, churn of new business formation and failure was relatively predictable: Each $1BB of spending drove roughly ~13 new construction businesses formed each year. This held even during volatile times (GFC, etc). Construction business was a SCALING exercise, not a 'INNOVATION' exercise. 

By ~2016-19, labor shortages + low interest rates drove increased pace of startups in construction. During this time, each $1BB of spend drove 17 construction startups (+27% higher vs norm). This was when Katerra, et al appeared - moonshots with moderate understanding of the industry, but generally poor framework of underlying business risk of going 'upstream' in production process. Enabled by low cost of capital.

Post-COVID, a labor shortage, pandemic, and ultra-easy funding drove construction startup rate to nearly 20 startups per $BB of spend (+15% above Katerra era), of all varieties of abilities. As the industry softened, new startups competed for fewer dollars (+22 new startups per $BB of spend...64% higher than historical norms), before pulling back due to tightening industry conditions.

Fast forward to 2026, and a new surge of construction startups (conceivably tied to AI) is underway. Some of this is tied to datacenters, but also includes startups in other areas. +22% higher YOY pace of startup per $$ YOY (22 startups per $BB of spend). Near all time highs.

Why this matters:

1) New entrants mean relationships and market share shuffle. These companies will procure differently. 'Old relationships' matter less.  
2) Arguably, a signal of increased innovation ahead. Simply more firms entering, and some will succeed and do things differently. Much needed in construction.
3) After ~3 years of industry softening, change is occurring (a bit like how resale housing seems to be 'clearing' at the margin with higher volumes but soft prices. This is healthy in the macro, but can be risky in the 'micro'.

Such interesting (historical?) times underway in the industry.

$73B of deferred home improvement...I like the simplicity of this analysis of deferral. From our forecast report. Several points:

1) Remodel spend surged +43% during COVID (2020-22), but roughly half of that growth was in prices (as occurs during shortages). 

Remember when surging lumber prices was mainstream feature on Odd Lots with Joe Weisenthal? Shortages drove unusual pricing. Ditto with window/door prices, labor, etc. 

2) From peak spend (2022) to today, volumes declined roughly -19%. We break this down by tier. As you might expect, deferral looks different by category.

3) But in that time, underlying occupied housing stock which underpin spend grew by +11%. Some of that is new build, but the count of homes 'aging in' to replacement years from the mid-2000's actually grew even faster. There should be +11% more spending than 2019 levels in 2026, minimum.

Now for outlier factors:
Replacement cycles shifted due to longer lived materials. Great innovations to better building materials drove a knock-on shift in timing of spend. We believe $20B incremental deferral just in 2026 from underlying product shifts.

As a case study, this happened in reroof when roofs that should have been replaced 2014-19 were pushed to 2020-25 due to better-aging asphalt. 

Now this is playing out for other segments that are easier to defer.
- Lighting
- Flooring
- Windows
- Decking
- etc

A few products like appliances and plumbing have shorter replacement cycles. But that's an analysis for another day.

Now the good news:
Deferral is a really unusual phenomenon. Like roofing, it makes the industry look 'broke' for a period (no growth) until all of a sudden volumes begin to shift. In the case of discretionary spending (like kitchens), this results in much more lumpy/rapid growth when spending growth resumes.

As long as uncertainty is elevated/worsening, deferral continues. We can't predict global stability, and pricing is getting more complicated (also a topic for another post). That said, if you believe uncertainty eventually eases, you also need to believe that when growth resumes, it likely recovers faster than mid-low single digits, simply because of the unusual deferral dynamic. To ignore that is a big mistake.

What an intriguing backdrop to digest QXO / HD / LOW results in August. The industry should be watching for stabilization, because the implication to the industry longer term is not 'steady', but 'turning'.


PS: I've seen analysis of home improvement which ignore pricing (or worse...use CPI as a deflator which was historically fine tool, but not during a lumber shortage). Be careful - pull forward is an analysis of volume.

PPS: When deferred volume 'turns' positive, there is a case that most of the volume shows up as 'pro jobs' (driven by demographics of older homeowners who skew PRO and prefer not to DIY, as well as complexity of deferred jobs). If these jobs are funded by HELOC (plausible in 2027), the type of contractor also changes.

Throwback: ~ 2 years ago we calculated only ~5% of building product brands would actually have meaningful pricing power amid softening consumer outlook. 

Another ~20% would muddle along but manage. The other 75% would likely struggle to hold margins/market share.

the issue was 'pro veto', where pro contractors have meaningful sway on what product actually gets installed. 

In practice, what happens is something that looks like:
a) Homeowner loves the product, but the pro installer prefers another some reason (familiar, more reliable, better margin, etc). reasons can vary, but the common thread is 'VETO'.

b) Pro VETO defaults to the supplier preferred by the pro (rank order number one). Usually a very thin set of competitors.

c) The product is close enough that the homeowner simply rolls over. But the shift can be meaningful (different material, different solution, almost always a different brand)

Why its hard:
a) Often the 'VETO' is very geographically isolated. A toehold hard to identify unless leadership is very canny. Think of a pocket in the west coast or northeast that suddenly skews different. 

b) Pro 'VETO' often involves material substitutions - countertop materials, flooring materials, different solutions in roofing or plumbing. consumers don't push material conversions on their own. This takes time for manufacturers to perceive. 

c) In practice, pro-VETO tends to be very sticky. Really hard to uproot, and requires deliberate effort (not simple price increase/decreases). Usually outside the typical product manager 'toolkit'. For example, one company physically took management on an RV on a roadtrip ('grassroots' efforts with pro contractors) to hit the region in question at their jobsites. Its...messy and uncertain from ROI standpoint.

Why this matters now:
a) conversions between alternative materials or products is...changing. Industry is less confident on the underlying math outlining long-term material shifts.

b) Distribution is changing for the impacted categories, all rooted around the notion that substitution is fairly manageable and led by the brand. This typically breaks regionally.

c) Rampant attempts at price increases, but very unevenly deployed, and clearly limited visibility into real elasticities, which are skewed.

d) It seems (personal observation) these veto problems start at the 'top' pricepoint (luxury starting to rebound), and then filter to other tiers. That lingering issue gets more pronounced 12 months out.

Such interesting times to be in housing/building products.

BTW - side note: There are some intriguing math scaling principles at play here (also observed in other industries), regarding who actually captures margin in the industry. The punchline is most of the margin gains gets accrued in a few winners while the rest struggle to hold margin or market share.

Building Product leaders should pay attention: Green categories below will have more predictable pricing integrity over the summer months. Red will suffer. This is real data, collected at time of home configuration.

Categories in red are facing pricing headwinds, because consumers have limited dollars to deploy, and are selecting the product as part of a larger 'bundle' of other products. Fighting for fewer dollars.
- Flooring
- Lighting
- Faucets
- Hardware
- Cabinet
- Plumbing

The above categories have 5x more dispersion in pricing, due to net substitution. Consumers are being offered lower priced options as part of the bundle, with some manufactures are getting lost in the process. 

In contrast, categories in GREEN facing much more predictable pricing.
- Exterior finish (siding, etc) - no surprise there.
- Interior finish
- Windows/doors
- Structural upgrades
- Appliances.

Remember that products selected today turn into revenue in ~3-4 months. 
Our forecast drops shortly. The pricing is always the toughest part (and like all forecasters, we will be wrong). Data like this helps us course correct early.

Our new forecast drops later this week. Beyond the macro, here are 10 product-specific themes impacting revenues but are generally being missed in forecast discussions.

Siding – Much more skewed by production / custom mix than perceived. Seeing greater ‘multi-material’ siding combos among top ~20 builders, which reduces effective volume of siding sold for ‘winners’ who are only capturing part of the home (less addressable sq ft)

Windows – Mix specific issues developing. Historically, windows/doors gained share of R&R during recessions (attractive financing + savings on home energy costs). Now it seems an unusual deferral picture developing vs other segments (more deferral), which potentially skews timing towards greater rebound ahead. Conflict / supply chain challenges make sourcing of components/hardware more interesting.

Roofing – I take the ‘over’ for elevated storm damage late 2026, but in context of longer-term demand (say 2030+) converging closer to 2018 levels due to bizarre deferral of reroof from material shift. Future roofing probably looks less like ‘reroof’ and more like ‘major remodel + reroof’, which has implications for distribution and pro capture. 

Decking – Decking R&R is really ‘lagged new construction’ over the past ~5 years. The industry should be asking better questions about penetration math of composite materials, and where marginal gains occur next.

Outdoor living- Driven by density and affordability challenges (home configuration shift). What’s happening in master-planned communities in 2026 becomes outdoor living revenue in 2028.

Appliances – One of the few categories with SHRINKING average product life, and arguably a better medium-term deferral picture than most. Luxury appliances is one of the more interesting segments to monitor.

Luxury – Luxury has the most deferral of any segment, and historically turned positive ~18 months before any broader industry recovery. Winning luxury means winning the pro who can ‘veto’ the consumer perception.

Flooring – Flooring upgrades lower, but some evidence of other shift underway (perception shift of LVP and some carpets changing?) Every other category should root for flooring upgrades, which drive ~1.5x higher mix benefit to other unrelated categories who get upgraded along with the floors. 

Kitchens / Baths – by far, the most sensitive to income elasticity (and oil price effects). Mix shift / substitution issues developing in underlying materials. Plumbing products also have shorter avg life in 2026, which implies K&B growth comes from bathroom segment first due to issues with scaling.

Insulation – What an interesting category. Pricing volatility, datacenter exposure, and indirectly the more cyclical of the bunch due to new res and HELOC exposure from additions.

A particularly challenging time for oil price volatility to occur, but we expect conditions to play out very differently by segment. Much more to come.

Field notes while traveling: these homes in Montenegro were built 13 years apart. Can you tell? Can you spot the difference between US homes built in 2013 vs 2026? 

Suppose interest rates fell by ~200 basis points, would you expect the same knock-on effect in home improvement spend for this housing markets as the US? That would be unreasonable. Why this matters:

The same principle of shift in economic sensitivity is playing out in the US, albeit more modestly. For example:
- Incandescent to LED light fixitures
- Carpet to longer-lived floors (LVP, tile, etc)
- Wood decking to composite decking
- REDUCTION of lifespan in appliances and plumbing, resulting in more frequent spend on those categories
- Shift to architectural roofing and metal roofs
- And a number of other shifts in usage.

Key insight here is that small differences in allocation of capital vs labor (impacted by demographics, interest rates, local materials, etc) results in far different flavor of fluctuations and growth in later housing / home improvement cycles.

There are economic models being used right now within building product companies, including some investors, which essentially assume fixed effects (e.g. calibrated to sensitivity of ‘carpets’ but not ‘hard floors’ to swings in rates, incomes, etc). Simply because most of these models are backward calibrated. After all - historical data is the best (only) gauge to start with, but is imperfect when transitions like this occur.

As a result, spending has been slower to recover than older models might have anticipated, but make sense given context of the shift underway. It also means spending on home improvement gets a bit more cyclical the next cycle vs prior cycles, which has all sorts of implications for the scale and type of companies best suited to gain market share profitably.

The point is this:
Building materials distribution / suppliers for those identical-looking houses is structured nothing like the US because the local housing market cycles entirely differently with quite different underlying economics.

What the industry is learning in 2026+ is that housing suppliers will likely skew more remodeling focused, stock different mix/exposure products vs new build, and more (including leverage/etc)

New forecast published later this month. As we articulated earlier, such exciting transformation in building products / housing.
